title: Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux
summary:
The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load.

Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs.

To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko, an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year.

In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild.

Reviewing code is hard

Reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code.

To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative:

  1. LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence.
  2. LLMs are easier to bias. The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way.
  3. LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. No sane human can review the same patch applied to 100 slightly different branches to find the few that have incompatible changes.

How Sashiko reviews a patch

To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs, and requires each pass to record what it ruled out:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Gather context and plan\r\n -> Parallel specialist sessions (concerns + dismissed concerns)\r\n -> Triage\r\n -> Per-bug deep checks\r\n -> Review report'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f25d2236c50>)])]>

Notes on each step:

  1. Gather context and plan: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity.

  2. Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion.

  3. Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it.

  4. Per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding.

  5. Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list.

All this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many important contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev. Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code.

What the data shows

The real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions.

It is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. In fact, LWN.net recently wrote that Sashiko has already become an important part of the kernel's development process and was the top bug reporter of issues in the 7.2 release cycle.

It prevents new bugs and uncovers old ones. When Sashiko flags a bug in a proposed patch, the author typically fixes it in the next revision before the change is ever merged. Many developers run Sashiko locally or in corporate private instances. The bugs that Sashiko helped to prevent leave no trace in the git commit log, making them hard to count directly. What can be counted are fixes for preexisting bugs that Sashiko finds and reports as a byproduct of reviewing new changes: Sashiko is cited in over 2000 mainline kernel commits and in over 500 of this year's official Linux kernel CVEs, spanning drivers, core kernel code, networking, GPUs, memory management, and virtualization.

Fewer bugs are slipping into mainline releases. Across the 18 kernel releases prior to Sashiko (Linux 6.2 through 6.19, covering 254000 commits), an average of 3.4% of merged commits required a follow-up fix within 60 days. Since Sashiko rolled out, that 60-day fix rate has fallen to 2.8% in Linux 7.1 and 2.2% in Linux 7.2, a 35% drop (with the 30-day fix rate falling from 2.3% to 1.4%). It’s too early to make strong claims, and obviously many other factors can influence release-to-release numbers, so we cannot solely credit Sashiko for the entire drop, but the trend is optimistic.

Since Sashiko was rolled out, the percentage of merged commits in the Linux kernel that received a follow-up fix in 60 days has dropped by 35%.

A clean review carries real signal. If Sashiko's warnings were mostly noise, commits merged with warnings would need follow-up fixes no more often than commits that passed cleanly. In practice, across 21,500 tracked mainline commits, patches that received a clean Sashiko review required a follow-up fix within 60 days just 0.9% of the time — less than a third of the historical baseline. Patches merged despite a critical Sashiko warning needed a fix 7.6% of the time — an 8x higher risk (and 6.3x higher even after adjusting for patch size). 

That gap is what makes Sashiko useful to maintainers: A clean pass instills real confidence, while a critical warning is a strong reason to take another look at the proposed patch.

This all tracks with what Linus Torvalds wrote in a mailing-list discussion a few weeks after Sashiko’s launch:

"As you say, Sashiko tends to be quite good. Even when it flags something unnecessarily and there's no actual problem, there's likely to be a reason for the question. And we've seen some truly stellar reports too. Things that are deep and subtle, and the AI is 100% correct. So anybody who thinks that all AI is slop is in denial about the current state." - Linus Torvalds (on lore.kernel.org)

What we learned from building and running Sashiko

First, benchmark-driven development beats intuition. While developing Sashiko, we tried many ideas that looked very reasonable on their face but didn’t end up working out. Other ideas were less obvious but worked surprisingly well. What was crucial: Early on, we built a benchmark out of nearly 1,000 real Linux kernel bugs and used it to evaluate every major Sashiko change. Every bug in this set was a real mistake that had passed human review by kernel experts, had been merged into mainline Linux, and later had to be fixed. On that benchmark, Sashiko with the new Gemini 4 Carbon model catches 75.8% of the bugs that human reviewers missed (using high thinking level).

Second, coding agents are not great at reviewing their own code. Models are trained to produce a working solution within a limited token budget. Asking these agents to review their own code might work well for isolated tasks, but for real, large codebases, creating a functional solution is often just 5-10% of the work. What’s really hard is to produce a solution that works all of the time, is well-integrated into the surrounding code, and doesn’t introduce subtle regressions. This is often substantially more complex and requires additional effort. Similar to human developers, agents benefit from external code review: Reviewers often spot issues that the initial author missed, even if they are not more experienced.

Third, open source and shared community ownership and development help to build trust. By being fully open and transparent from the beginning, Sashiko allowed anyone to run it the way they wanted: using different models (including open source and local models), customizing prompts, or even adopting Sashiko to other-than-Linux projects. This helped with community adoption and brought over 100 contributors to improve Sashiko, including some prominent kernel developers.

More and more engineers are putting local Sashiko instances into their coding-agent loops, so patches are checked against the community's review rules before a human maintainer ever sees them. We use the same workflow to build Sashiko itself ("Sashiko for Sashiko"), running it to review every change to its codebase and prompt pipeline both locally and through a Github integration.

Although Sashiko started in the Linux kernel, the need for an agentic trust layer applies across critical open-source software. Because the core review engine does not depend on C or on kernel-specific rules, the Linux kernel playbook (combining an open verification pipeline, community-owned domain guides, and a benchmark mined from historically known issues and fixes) can likely be applied to other foundational open-source projects such as GCC, LLVM, or Git.

"Now, I think the other side of AI - and this is where Sashiko comes in - is that it basically does end up being a tool that can then increase the trust in the patch. So AI giveth, and AI taketh away. But the basic issue shouldn't be AI per se, it should be that notion of 'trust'." - Linus Torvalds on LKML

You can check out Sashiko at sashiko.dev, or find the code on GitHub to run it in your own development workflow.

title: Show HN: WebCraft Pro – CI-enforced engineering standards for AI coding agents
story_key: story|variant:pro|title:webcraft pro ci enforced engineering standards for ai coding agents
content_excerpt: A framework-agnostic engineering toolkit for AI agents. 40 skills, 8 stages, and strict CI pipelines (Node.js security linter + Playwright accessibility checks) to build secure, accessible, and high-craft web apps. WebCraft Pro is an open-source, framework-agnostic collection of 43 reusable Agent Skills , shared engineering standards, practical examples, and verification workflows for building distinctive, accessible, performant, and secure web applications. It provides AI coding agents with a structured engineering process covering the complete website delivery lifecycle—from initial design direction through implementation, accessibility, security, performance, browser QA, and release. The stage directories provide the roadmap, acceptance criteria, and supporting documentation. Canonical skills remain in skills/ , avoiding duplicated skill instructions across stages and AI agents. WebCraft Pro includes complementary GitHub Actions workflows and browser verification tooling. The Security Pattern Audit workflow runs a Node.js static pattern scanner built using Node.js standard-library modules. It checks for patterns including eval() , new Function() , unsafe innerHTML assignments, document.write() , potentially unsafe href values, and wildcard postMessage() origins. The workflow tests the scanner, generates a JSON report, verifies the report, and uploads it as an artifact. Scope limitation: This is a static Markdown code-example pattern audit—not a complete application security scanner or proof of security. The Accessibility Keyboard Tests workflow installs Chromium and executes the Playwright keyboard/focus test suite. The repository also includes an on-demand browser checker using Playwright and axe-core. This checker is available through the Manual Browser Check workflow. It is separate from the push-triggered keyboard-test workflow. Automated checks complement—not replace—manual assistive-technology testing, security review, cross-browser verification, and real-user performance measurement. Skills follow the Agent Skills format and are organized by task rather than tied to one frontend framework. The repository includes 13 practical templates across the three engineering-critical domains: These templates help agents and engineers record scope, test conditions, evidence, findings, remediation, and release decisions consistently. title: Parallel agent requests can slow down an Ollama session
story_key: story|title:parallel agent requests can slow down an ollama session
content_excerpt: Two coding-agent sessions sharing one Ollama slot waited a median 46 seconds for a response to start, against one second with a slot each. Over half the prompt tokens the server processed were repeats. Why hybrid models lose their place, and which settings change it. Ask a coding agent to fix a failing test. It might read a file, run the test, edit a function, then run the test again. Each time a tool returns a result, the agent sends another request to the model. From your terminal it looks like one conversation. From the server’s side it’s a series of increasingly long prompts, most of which it has already seen. Normally, that repetition is cheap. The server keeps the work it did on the previous turn and picks up where the new text begins. Now open a second terminal and give the same agent a task in another project. Both sessions send the same tool descriptions and much of the same setup text, but each has its own instructions and history. What happens to the first session’s work while the server answers the second? We tried this at Tensward with two unmodified Qwen Code sessions running against Ollama. When both sessions took turns on one slot (the place where the server holds an active request’s model state), the median request waited about 46 seconds for the response to start. When we gave each session a slot of its own, it waited about one second . Two sessions sharing a slot have to wait for each other. We expected some queueing. What surprised us in the logs was how much work the server did while they waited. With a shared slot, 54% of the prompt tokens it processed were repeats . With a slot each, that fell to 0.4%. Imagine pausing the server just after it reads token 8,921 of session A. Up to this point, sessions A and B are identical. The model is in exactly the state B needs. But the server keeps reading A, and B arrives only after A’s prompt is finished. Can the server get back to that moment? In a model that uses full causal attention throughout, the server keeps a pair of vectors for each token in each attention layer: a key and a value . Together these entries form the KV cache . Reading token 8,922 adds another entry. The entries for tokens 1 through 8,921 stay as they were, because earlier tokens cannot attend to later ones. As long as those entries are still in memory, the server can keep that prefix, discard A’s suffix, and start processing B where the prompts diverge. Qwen3.8-27B is a hybrid. Its full-attention layers have that same KV

title: LangSmith for Coding Agents: Now track spend by outcome
summary: LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce.
story_key: story|title:langsmith for coding agents now track spend by outcome
content_excerpt: Coding is the largest category of enterprise AI application spend, reaching $34B in 2026 . Every company now wants to know what all that spend returns, but most engineering leaders still can’t give an exact answer to what it's buying. To try to understand coding agent ROI, teams used to look at high-level data like usage analytics and AI consumption, but these don’t provide insight into what tokens actually produce. Answering the ROI question is hard and requires visibility into spend across users and teams, along with a way to connect it to outcomes. We felt this friction firsthand when spend with our own coding agent, Robin, started climbing, and is one of the reasons we built a model router. Now we're excited to offer a practical solution for our customers too. LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce. This provides a clearer way to calculate the ROI behind coding agent budgets and understand how changes to models and policies impact it. The new LangSmith Agent Platform operates around the agent. Each agent has its own record and belongs to an "agent type" that determines what its dashboard shows, which data it connects to, and how it's evaluated. Coding agents are the first specialized agent type, and present data on pull requests, one of the signs that the agent's work is useful. LangSmith already traces coding agents across model providers, including Claude Code and Codex . With coding agents in LangSmith, the spend in each trace is automatically attributed to pull requests each agent contributed to. The attribution reflects the tasks a coding agent is used for. It covers both cases where a single thread can open several PRs, and where a PR can take several threads to finish, so data in LangSmith reflects what your agents actually accomplished and what it cost. Up until today, LangSmith enabled you to see the cost per trace for any of your coding agents, one trace at a time. This is useful for manual debugging, but doesn't provide visibility into trends across the entire team. The new coding agent overview page aggregates those costs and ties them to the pull requests your agents worked on. The dashboard shows KPIs at a glance, and clicking any metric opens its trend over time. For example, if your team switched models, you can compare before and after to see the impact of the change. title: Introducing Unity Gateway Insights
summary: When looking to cut AI costs, teams often start with budgets or open-source models....
story_key: story|title:introducing unity gateway insights
content_excerpt: When looking to cut AI costs, teams often start with budgets or open-source models. But agent traces can reveal other opportunities to save. At Databricks, trace analysis surfaced several: offline replays showed no performance gain from upgrading from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, so we stayed on the cheaper 4.8; fixing common MCP errors recovered an estimated $1.2M in costs a year ; and traces showed that simple prompts were going to expensive models, prompting us to adopt Smart Routing . Today, we’re introducing Unity Gateway Insights , which automatically uses Genie to analyze millions of agent traces alongside your business data and ontology. It surfaces where tokens are being wasted: MCP errors that keep recurring, simple tasks running on expensive frontier models, and repeated workflows worth turning into shared skills, all in the context of your business and under the same governance as your other data. If you already have traffic flowing through Unity Gateway, open AI Gateway > Observability > Insights and generate a report for the last day, 7 days, or 30 days. Insights then writes a report on the tokenomics of your coding agent rollout that answers the following questions: You can add up to 10 questions of your own to a report, such as whether the newest model is worth it for your team's work. To dig further, continue the conversation with Genie. Ask which MCP server wasted the most tokens this month and who owns it, and you have a bug report ready to send. Finding this kind of waste requires a full record of every step of every agent session: inputs and outputs, tool calls, subagents, intermediate steps, latency, and token cost. A standalone gateway records only the requests that pass through it. Capturing the rest of each session means instrumenting every coding agent yourself, then exporting the traces to a data platform to analyze them. Pointing Claude Code at those traces still leaves you to design the investigation yourself, with no map of your business like the Genie Ontology provides. Insights runs the investigation we developed while rolling out coding agents to thousands of Databricks engineers. It samples sessions and groups them into workstreams by kind of work. Then it checks each workstream for failing MCP tools, bloated context, frontier models on simple tasks, and repeated workflows, and ranks what it finds by the tokens at stake. title: Keeping Agents Fast: High-Interactivity Decode with FlyDSL MonoKernels in vLLM
summary: How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration.
story_key: model:vllm|title:keeping agents fast high interactivity decode with flydsl monokernels in vllm
content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. title: Bitter lessons we learned from building an open-source coding agent
story_key: story|title:bitter lessons we learned from building an open source coding agent
content_excerpt: When I was a kid, I really wanted to jailbreak my iPod so I could play Gameboy games on it. I got good enough at it that I turned it into a little business: people would hand me their devices and I’d jailbreak them. The business eventually went under because I dropped my backpack and broke a bunch of phones inside. But I got Gameboy games on my iPod, so as far as I was concerned, all was good. Eventually I decided I wanted to build my own games, so I took a programming class in high school. I always liked just tinkering with a little thing, and that little thing was software. So what’s been exciting to me about LLMs and agents is a very simple feeling: wow, I can build so many more things. The nature of how we build software has changed really fast, and all the random ideas that come to me in the shower that’d I’d normally never get around to suddenly felt doable. If I’m honest, Sculptor didn’t start with some big idea. Just: can we help people build more things? I first got access to real LLMs with the GPT-4 API. One of the first things I tried was modeled on a paper called ReAct — the basic idea of giving an agent access to tools, bash commands, roughly what you see in claude code today. At the time, it was too early. LLMs weren’t good enough and it didn’t work. I went down the obvious path: okay, what if I built more scaffolding around the model? To make up for the model’s weaknesses, I could build more tooling. So we (at this time, it was just me and Josh, Imbue’s CTO) built a tool called Crafty. Crafty let you generate code in parallel - at the time we didn’t have agents, just API calls to GPT that returned diffs. I really cared about parallelism: while the model is off doing its work, you shouldn’t be sitting at your screen watching it. You should be building the next thing. Then we ran into the bitter lesson of AI, which is: any investment you build around the model tends to lose out to plain improvements in the model itself. We were building tools so that a model could do a simple task like fixing the bugs that a linter flags, but pretty soon the model could just do it on its own. The scaffolding we built was useless. I was sad. But lessons were learned. Next we built something very, very complicated, and we called it Blackberry. OpenAI had an internal project codenamed Strawberry at the time, so we thought it’d be funny. The concept was: What if you wrote the commit messages for your feature ahead of time ? title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
story_key: story|ver:180|variant:moe|title:180b parameters 32gb of ram pushing moe inference to the limit with transformers
content_excerpt: Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. title: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages
story_key: story|ver:0.5|variant:flash,speech|title:rumble 2 flash an open 0 5b speech model for 40 languages
content_excerpt: Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code . To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip. On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities. On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER . Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx . That's an hour of audio in about half a second. Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER , on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better. The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash . It's also available through our API . We're very curious what you'll b

title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
summary: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.

title: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition
summary:
Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed.
  We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.

title: Learning Stratified Policies for Inference-Time Objectives
summary: Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective. We realize this policy population using separate LoRA adapters on a shared language model backbone and optimize it for pass@$k$. We theoretically motivate the approach by analyzing the linear setting; a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error in settings where every single LoRA has strictly positive prediction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that stratified policies consistently improve pass@$k$ over a single-policy baseline across multiple reasoning tasks. Overall, our results highlight how distributing samples across complementary policies can be a more effective use of sample budget than repeated i.i.d. sampling from a single policy at inference time.

title: Paul Stack: I'll Never Write Infrastructure as Code Again
summary:
Paul Stack helped build Terraform. Now he says he'll never write another line of infrastructure as code, because an agent harness runs his team's production infrastructure instead.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:

Then stay for Paul's full DevCon talk, From Page to Dossier, on a lights-out factory that does the 3am on-call legwork before anyone is woken up.

title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
summary: AlphaProof Code agents wrote three  million lines of proofs in Lean to verify Signal’s core encryption.
story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices.   • Fixed deny rules not being applied to a permission approval that arrives after Claude Code restarts, in self-hosted runner and claude remote-control sessions
  • Fixed a case where a committed .claude/settings.local.json could be treated as the user's own when Claude Code was started in certain subfolders of a repository
  • Fixed some deny and ask rules not applying to certain Bash commands
  • Fixed a gap in Bash permission checks where some compound commands could run without asking; these now ask for permission
  • Fixed a case where a Bash allow rule could run a different program than the one it names
  • Fixed a connector tool's approval prompt in cloud sessions being answered automatically while plugins were still loading
  • Fixed some subagents changing an artifact that people outside your organization can see, or uploading files to it, without asking first when an allow rule is set or uploads were approved earlier
  • Fixed some artifact publishes skipping the confirmation for pages that people outside your organization can see when "don't ask again" had been chosen for Artifact
  • Fixed auto mode judging only the first change to an artifact that people outside your organization can see; its yes now covers that change alone
  • Fixed a managed strictPluginOnlyCustomization lock on agents and skills not taking effect in sessions that were already running
  • Fixed sandboxed commands being able to write to the native updater's download folder in some cases
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a worktree's settings and hooks
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a linked worktree's shared git folder
  • Fixed /teleport's stash choice in some unusual git states: it now stops and says what to do
  • Windows: Fixed a start-up stall that could last about a second when a PATH entry sits under a folder your account cannot open
  • Fixed /resume on Windows refusing or hiding sessions whose folder was recorded with a different drive-letter case or slashes
  • Fixed an in-session /resume on Windows dropping a project's saved trust when the session was recorded with a different drive-letter case
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when the working directory was below an allowRead folder inside a denyRead, such as under a symlinked home directory
  • Fixed Claude Desktop's third-party deployments staying on "Stopping" until a token renewal finished (once it includes this version)
  • Improved subagents cut off at the output token limit: they are now asked for the whole answer again, more briefly, instead of returning only its end
  • Improved startup with a keyless Console sign-in or other Anthropic profile login: a token that is still valid is read without waiting for the credentials lock
  • Improved the account email check: it now also refuses your email as a client's identity in scripts a command runs, file writes, web fetches and MCP calls
  • Improved the HTTPS authentication failed message for private plugin marketplaces: it now says git's terminal prompts and askpass programs are disabled, and it also appears with newer git versions
  • Improved the add-marketplace confirmations, plugin recommendation prompts and plugin install warning to say that plugins can run code on your computer, with access to your files and shell
  • Improved the claude --desktop sign-in error to name the API key, provider or setting that stops a Claude account sign-in from working
  • Improved the /voice "No audio detected" message on macOS and Windows: it now says where to pick your microphone
  • Improved MCP tasks: Claude is now told when a task is waiting for your answer, and can point you to /tasks
  • Improved claude remote-control: it now exits with status 4 when it stops by itself (single-session runs still exit 0) and 69 when it can't register, so a service manager can start it again
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session can't use its session's API key or token: they no longer suggest adding the key to settings
  • Improved the bundled dataviz skill's part-to-whole advice for static images and for parts with a natural order, such as age bands
  • Changed sandboxed Bash commands to follow the normal permission flow by default; set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true to keep running them without prompts
  • Changed managed settings that turn the sandbox on: to keep commands running without prompts, set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true in your highest-ranking managed source
  • Changed read-only git commands to ask first in a repository that isn't the project's or one you trusted; name it with --add-dir, not the additionalDirectories setting, to run them without prompts
  • Changed scheduled tasks and /loop to ask before running a skill that declares allowed-tools or hooks; add Skill(name) to permissions.allow to run it unattended
  • Changed "Always allow" in Desktop, IDE and SDK hosts: a rule alone is offered only when saving it would allow that command again, so a scheduled task that relied on one can now wait for you
  • Changed the sandbox to refuse sandboxed writes to .claude settings, skills, agents, commands and hooks in added directories, as it does in the launch folder
  • Changed worktree isolation: an isolated worktree session or agent is now refused git bisect run, git maintenance register|start and scalar's set-up commands, and is told what still works
  • Changed plugin MCP bundles (.mcpb, .dxt) to unpack under the plugins directory, not .mcpb-cache in the plugin's folder, so read-only plugin folders load; one fetched by URL downloads again once
  • Changed plugins of a remote marketplace that managed settings declare, enable and list in prependPlugins or appendPlugins to count as the organization's; pluginDigests is deprecated and ignored
  • Changed plugin loading to skip, and claude plugin validate to report, some unsafe paths and links in a plugin's folder
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders in --plugin-dir plugins no longer load from a session started above them; start Claude Code in the plugin folder instead
  • Changed EnterWorktree to refuse a WorktreeCreate hook path that goes through a symlink inside the project; have the hook print the real path
  • Changed tmux and iTerm2 teammates, and new sessions from the agents view opened with ←, to start in the session's folder instead of where the shell last ran cd
  • Changed prompt suggestions in the terminal to refresh less often after 8 turns in a row started by background or scheduled tasks, saving usage until you press a key or return to the terminal
  • Changed Esc on a background MCP task's question to "answer later": nothing is sent to the server, and the question stays in /tasks
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS to also set the context window of unrecognized model IDs that start with claude-, such as a gateway's claude-sonnet-latest
  • Changed /login to ask for permission to change your privacy settings
  • Changed /cost, $.session.usage(), --max-budget-usd and the cost and token metrics to count a mod's $.model.complete and $.model.classify calls
  • Changed the programs that Claude Code's sandbox starts for its own use, such as its network bridge, to run without Claude Code's sign-in tokens and API keys in their environment
  • Changed ripgrep, local git commands and the sandbox runtime's own helper programs to run without the mTLS client key's passphrase in their environment
  • Remote Control: Changed /resume and /teleport to disconnect first when the connected session has a share link, or when that can't be checked; run /remote-control to connect again
  • Changed Claude Code on the web, cloud scheduled tasks and Cowork cloud sessions to start despite sandbox.failIfUnavailable: the hosted container has no command sandbox
  • Changed requests for settings, permission rules, hooks or status over a cloud or self-hosted session's connection to return less or be refused; what applies in the session is unchanged
  • Changed claude -p with no cached account data to wait for that data before its first request, so a first run in a clean environment can start a few seconds later
  • Changed Claude's instructions to keep files you'll want out of its temporary scratchpad folder, which can be cleared
  • Changed marketplace ref to accept the full ID of any commit on a branch or tag; clients before this version can't clone such a pin, so a marketplace pinned this way stops loading there
  • Changed plugin marketplace and plugin downloads to use a CONNECT tunnel when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy set; a proxy that refuses CONNECT now fails them
  • Changed -p and SDK runs in a worktree or submodule mounted into a container to apply .claude/settings.local.json allow rules only once the folder is trusted
  • Changed self-hosted runners to refuse a session whose session folder or repository path is a symbolic link, other than a checkout hook's checkout
  • Removed "ask your admin to raise it" from spend limit and shared budget errors in cloud sessions and under Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Added prompt suggestions wherever the terminal shows them: Tab accepts the suggested next prompt; promptSuggestionEnabled: false in Claude Code's settings.json turns them off
  • [VSCode] Added a Console sign-in that creates no API key
  • [VSCode] Added a field to paste the redirect URL when signing in to an MCP server from the panel in SSH, WSL and container windows
  • [VSCode] Fixed the model picker's check mark staying on the old model after Claude Code restarted on another model or the model was switched over Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Fixed the effort selector offering levels above the effort cap set by your organization or the maxEffortLevel setting
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen offering sign-ins that the managed allowedProviders setting refuses
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for MCP tools not saying why Claude Code asks when a safety check raises the question
  • [VSCode] Fixed the message for organization settings that couldn't load saying to run a command again; it now says to try again, matching the tab's Retry link
  • [VSCode] Improved the note shown for an untrusted folder: it now says why the extension is off and how to turn it on
  • [VSCode] Improved the error shown when the system refuses to run Claude Code: it now says your IT team can allow a blocked program
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in card to say what to do when the browser shows a connection error for localhost
  • [VSCode] Changed the install link's marketplace confirmation button to "Trust marketplace and continue"
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed new cloud sessions cutting MCP tool descriptions loaded through tool search at 4,096 characters; the limit is now 16,384, as in other Claude Code sessions
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed artifact links pasted in Slack getting no card when the poster's Claude sign-in had expired in a workspace their organization doesn't manage; a plain card now appears

Added a spinner tip in VS Code and similar integrated terminals about re-running a notebook cell, shown once Claude has read or edited a Jupyter notebook
